The Kings of the Persians.
that he should go and heal him,
and he would give him half of his kingdom.
And he did not go,
because a reward was promised to him.
Now these books of his are extant:
The Book of Aphorisms;
The Book of Prognostics;
The Book of Arsanā {OCR? Ars amandi? / Fractures?};
The Book of Humours (chyme?);
The Book of the Belly (gaster;
that is, the belly,
stomach?);
The Book of Waters and Air;
The Book of the Nature of Man;
The Book of Wounds of the Head;
The Book of the Testament.
After Darius, Xerxes his son [ruled] twenty-one years.
And in his second year he conquered Egypt.
And in the eleventh year he came to Athens
and burned it with fire.
And in his time,
when Haman the Amalekite sought to destroy the Jews who remained in the captivity,
Esther and Mordecai put on sackcloth,
and the Lord turned Haman's evil back upon his own head.
And some say
that if this affair had taken place at this time,
Ezra would not have remained silent from mentioning it,
since he wrote about everything belonging to that time.
[Artaxerxes ruled] seven months,
and they are counted with the years of Xerxes.
[Longimanus ruled] forty-one years.
And in his seventh {OCR? 5} year,
he commanded Ezra the scribe to go up and build Jerusalem,
that is to say, the city, after the temple had been built.
And a vision of God appeared to Ezra the scribe,
and he rewrote the scriptures {OCR?} from memory,
because their books had been burned in the captivity.
And in his twentieth year, Nehemiah the cupbearer was sent to rebuild Jerusalem again.
He, although a Hebrew by race, was a confidant and cupbearer of Artaxerxes;
and he petitioned the king and the queen, and went up.
And when the Jews did not have holy fire in Jerusalem,
because they had cast it into a well when they were taken captive,
Nehemiah gave orders, and they brought some of the mud from that well and cast it upon the wood of the burnt offerings,
and it caught fire after one hundred and forty-six years.
Now Nehemiah himself remained in Jerusalem for twelve years.
And from this time of Artaxerxes, Africanus reckons the seventy weeks that are written of in Daniel,
which make four hundred and ninety years,
and they end in the year three hundred and sixty-six of the Greeks,
in the second year of Nero,
in whose days Jerusalem was besieged.
Thus far.
